title: Newton's law of gravitation and field strength; Coulomb's law
source: Questions copied unchanged from the mission-lesson scripts for Eduqas A-level Physics (status of the source: mission-lesson scripts of Oct-Nov 2026 (reviewed by AI reviewers; not signed off by a person)). Terms and clues: C03-uk1#t3 term and clue written for the game; F02-1#t2 term and clue written for the game; C03-uk1#t1 term and clue written for the game; F02-1#t1 term and clue written for the game. Questions: C03-uk1#N.3, F02-1#N.4, C03-uk1#N.8, F02-1#N.8a, C03-uk1#N.9a, F02-1#N.12b.

assemble.prompt: Match each term to its definition.

items.label: Vector
items.clue: Quantity that has both a size and a direction.

items.label: Repulsion
items.clue: What happens between like charges, such as two positive ones.

items.label: Force field
items.clue: Region in which a body experiences a non-contact push or pull.

items.label: Coulomb's law
items.clue: Rule that two point charges interact in proportion to their product and to 1/r².

questions.stem: Which statement is true for the gravitational field of a point mass but not for the electric field of a point charge?

options.text: The field strength is inversely proportional to the square of the distance from the source.
The force on any test object placed in the field is always towards the source.
The field strength is defined as force per unit of a property of a small test object.
The field lines around the source are radial straight lines.

questions.explanation: Masses only attract, so the force always points to the source. An electric force on a test charge can point away from the source if the charges have the same sign.

questions.stem: Two small charged spheres whose centres are 0.60 m apart exert electric forces of magnitude 1.0 N on each other. Their charges do not change. At what centre-to-centre separation would the forces have a magnitude of 9.0 N?
Two electrons are held a short distance apart, far from all other objects. Which statement correctly describes the forces the electrons exert on each other?

options.text: They exert repulsive forces of both kinds, as their charges are alike.
Each electron repels the other electrically and attracts it gravitationally.
They exert only repulsive electric forces, having too little mass for gravity.
Their gravitational attraction exceeds their electric repulsion.

questions.stem: Three point charges are fixed on the x-axis: P (+4.0 nC) at x = 0, Q (+1.0 nC) at x = 0.10 m and R (+2.0 nC) at x = 0.30 m. Take 1/(4πε₀) = 8.99 × 10⁹ N m² C⁻². What is the magnitude of the resultant electric force on Q?
Two equal masses are fixed a distance d apart. Separately, a charge +Q and a charge −Q are fixed a distance d apart. Which statement about the resultant field at the midpoint of each pair is correct?

options.text: It is zero for both pairs.
It is zero for the masses; for the charges it is not zero and points towards −Q.
It is not zero for the masses; for the charges it is zero.
It is zero for the masses; for the charges it is not zero and points towards +Q.

questions.explanation: Gravity only attracts, so the two pulls at the midpoint are equal and opposite. A positive test charge there is pushed away from +Q and pulled towards −Q: both towards −Q.

questions.stem: Two small charged spheres exert electric forces of magnitude F on each other. The charge on each sphere is halved, and the distance between them is reduced to one third of its value. What is the magnitude of the force now?
questions.explanation: Force ∝ (product of the charges)/r². Charges: ½ × ½ = ¼. Distance: 1/(⅓)² = 9. New force = 9F/4 ≈ 2.3F.
